name: Elena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead six policy clerks at an insurer. I earn more than most clerks here because I catch changes to cover before renewal letters go out, and I never use AI tools. I rent alone, have no children and have saved about nine months of expenses. There are plenty of insurers nearby, though I still like to see a signed paper schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the policy team that the new sorter can file renewal letters, but people still need to read the exclusions. I do not use AI tools, and I would ask the clerks to keep the signed policy beside each change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead six clerks and earn above the usual rate because I catch policy changes that would leave a customer uncovered. I live alone, have nine months of expenses saved and see plenty of insurers nearby, so my own rent feels safe today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my Monday audit of twenty renewed policies and put 150 into savings each month while my salary holds. In the first year I would ask for paper copies of any automated change notices and check a sample against signed terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my current wage and flat. A renewal letter is only useful if the customer can see what changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changed in a real renewal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One customer lost cover for a bicycle after a small print change. I found it before the next payment and got the letter corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What paper would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the signed schedule with the audit file, not just the computer summary. That has saved us from arguing over an old version twice.

say: I would keep **signed policy terms** beside every automated renewal letter customers receive.
I would continue **Monday renewal audits** to catch changed exclusions before payment.
think: I have **nine months saved** and high pay for this job.
I do not use **AI tools** in my own work.
do: **Audit twenty renewals** each Monday against signed terms and changed exclusions.
**Save 150 monthly** while current pay continues and covers rent.
S0.quote: A renewal letter is only useful if the customer can see what changed.
fieldNote: Her **manual audit** catches changed exclusions before customers pay rather than merely filing renewals.
Her high pay and **nine-month reserve** support present security without implying permanent employment or new job offers.

steps.text: Audit twenty renewed policies each Monday against signed terms
Save 150 monthly while current salary continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say Steady Disruption puts renewal writing and checking straight into software, so the team needs a clear human appeal route. I would bring the staff association examples of changed exclusions and ask it to demand paid review hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead hours could shrink if one reviewer covers several offices, although I have nine months saved and several nearby employers. I would rather keep my hands on the signed schedule than learn an unproved tool under a new productivity target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take five anonymised renewal errors to the association meeting next month and request written staffing and appeal hours. I would keep auditing policies while paid; if my hours fall, I would check posted local policy-clerk jobs for actual salary and hours before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, even with savings. A list of nearby firms does not tell me which one is hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would the group ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask who can reverse a wrong renewal and how many paid hours remain to check changes. I would not promise the team that the association can force an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a real posted opening only if the net pay covers rent, food and travel. I would also ask whether the new employer uses the same automated renewal queue.

say: I would ask for **human renewal appeals** and paid review hours.
I would take **anonymised errors** to the association.
think: I could lose **lead hours** if renewal checks are merged.
I know **nearby insurers** may not have vacancies.
do: **Bring five renewal errors** to association meeting next month.
**Keep auditing policies** while the current role pays.
**Check real local openings** if hours fall and net pay covers essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts to her own hours.
S1.quote: A list of nearby firms does not tell me which one is hiring.
fieldNote: Her **association request** seeks paid review hours and a named appeal route, without assuming a concession.
Her **job search** requires an actual posted local role with enough net pay for rent, food and travel.

steps.text: Bring five anonymised renewal errors to association for paid review hours
Audit signed renewal terms while current role pays
Check posted local policy jobs if hours fall and net pay covers essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that AGI by 2028 could draft and check nearly all of our policy changes more cheaply than us. Robots dealing with physical damage may arrive around 2031, but our desk wages face the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead post could go, though no one has given me a cut notice. Nine months saved gives me time to look, but I still need paid work and cannot assume a similar role will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written staffing notice now and reserve the nine months of cash for rent rather than buy an AI course I do not trust. If my job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply only to advertised paid local policy appeal posts with net pay covering essentials and check public support rules if the search runs long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible loss of my own salary, but I have time and a search plan. Savings can hold my flat; they cannot keep a job open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a new post show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the salary, hours and actual appeal duties in writing. A post called policy reviewer could be a short contract with lower net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you counting on public help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count public money before the office confirms eligibility. I can spend my own reserve carefully while I find out.

say: I would warn that **policy desk wages** face AGI by 2028.
I would explain **physical robots arrive later**, around 2031.
think: I think my **lead post could go** without written notice.
I have **nine months saved**, but still need paid work.
do: **Request written staffing notice** and reserve cash for rent now.
Apply to **advertised appeals posts** after loss only if net wages cover essentials.
**Check support eligibility** if the search runs long.
feel: **Anxious** about possible salary loss, with time to search.
S2.quote: Savings can hold my flat; they cannot keep a job open.
fieldNote: She names **possible job loss** without a cut notice, and does not describe certain dismissal or sleeplessness.
Future **appeals work and support** depend on real local posts, sufficient net pay and confirmed eligibility.

steps.text: Request written staffing notice and preserve nine-month reserve for rent
Apply to advertised local policy appeals posts after loss if net pay covers essentials
Check public employment support eligibility if job search runs long

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 leaves time to put the renewal appeal rules in writing before software takes over the desk. Physical robots could follow around 2034, later than the policy work they cannot protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still do not want to spend evenings chasing a fashionable certificate. I could learn a proven appeals procedure if the insurer pays for it during work hours and preserves my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for two paid afternoon sessions with the appeals manager, using invented renewal disputes, only if my existing hours and salary are protected in writing. If approved I would practise the rule book and ask the association for annual paid-post counts; after 2031 loss I would seek a qualified local vacancy only if net pay covers rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual job risk, but the extra years let me ask for paid training. I will not spend the rent reserve on a course the company will not recognise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are those sessions available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager has not offered the sessions. If they are refused, I would continue the paid audit job and ask again when there is a real appeals opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would two sessions qualify you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two afternoons would show me the procedure, not make me a qualified lawyer. I would check the requirements in the vacancy notice before applying.

say: I would demand **paid appeals practice** with protected existing hours.
I would want **written renewal rules** before 2031.
think: I would try **proven training** if the insurer funds it.
I cannot assume **short practice** is a qualification.
do: **Request paid appeals sessions** only with salary and hours protected in writing.
**Practise invented disputes** if approved; ask for annual paid-post counts.
**Seek qualified local work** after 2031 loss only if net pay covers essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about later wage risk, with a funded route to test.
S3.quote: I will not spend the rent reserve on a course the company will not recognise.
fieldNote: Her **training is conditional** on paid time and written protection of salary and hours.
Later **appeals work** needs actual qualified openings and enough net income.

steps.text: Request two paid appeals sessions with salary and hours protected in writing
Practise invented renewal disputes only if sessions are approved
Ask association for annual paid appeals post counts
Seek qualified local vacancy after 2031 loss if net pay covers essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to save and make appeal rights plain. Robots handling physical damage may follow around 2039, while renewal paperwork changes earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel safe in my own work and rent for the next few years, although I am young enough to need another earning route eventually. Nine months saved is a useful base, not a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep Monday renewal audits and save 200 each month while the current high salary holds. I would ask the association each year for actual paid appeal vacancies; if my role ends after 2036, I would apply to qualified local posts only when net wages cover rent and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change but secure about the next few years. I can plan slowly without pretending a policy title lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for counts of paid hours, not just the number of appeals received. A queue can grow while the staff budget shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep renting unless a real offer and a written budget made a move sensible. Plenty of offices here is a reason to check nearby work first.

say: I would ask for **paid appeals hours** at local insurers before AGI reaches the desk in 2036.
I would keep **signed renewal audits** running while the present high-paid role lasts.
think: I feel **secure near term** on current pay and savings.
I still need **future earnings** beyond one policy title.
do: **Audit renewals Monday** and save 200 monthly while salary holds.
**Request annual vacancy counts** through the association.
**Apply locally after loss** only to qualified posts with bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Uneasy** later, secure for the next few years.
S4.quote: A queue can grow while the staff budget shrinks.
fieldNote: Her **near-term security** reflects above-typical pay, nine months saved and current paid work.
She treats **later vacancies** as conditional on qualification, actual posted openings and net wages covering essential bills.

steps.text: Audit signed policy renewals every Monday while present role pays
Save 200 monthly while current high salary continues
Ask staff association annually for paid appeals vacancies
Apply to qualified local post after 2036 loss if net pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the policy desk could shrink before I have tested any other paid work. Written notice, a qualified local offer with enough net pay and confirmed support rules would help me protect the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a customer knows a renewal has changed. I want the old and new cover on the same page, where a person can actually compare them.

headlineQuote: I want the old and new cover on the same page, where a person can actually compare them.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old policy lead** with a bachelor’s degree and above-typical pay.
She rents **alone**, has nine months saved and never uses AI tools.
She catches **changed exclusions** through signed schedules and favours association requests for paid appeals.
She considers **funded practice** only with protected hours and applies after loss only to qualified bill-covering posts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink the policy desk before she tests another paid route.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a qualified bill-covering local offer and confirmed support rules would help.
